records.name: Denmark
records.summary:
Denmark is a historically progressive destination. It was the first European country to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration (2014), has banned conversion therapy (2023), offers nonbinary gender markers, and has comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering gender identity. There is no rollback movement, and Copenhagen ranks among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities.

One documented weakness: the Danish Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that a trans woman who legally changed her gender but hasn't had surgery must serve in a men's prison and be strip-searched by male staff — finding this did not violate the European Convention on Human Rights. This is the same prison-placement issue documented in France, Germany, and the UK. The Danish Institute for Human Rights also flags that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time of reporting.

Anti-trans discourse is intensifying (debate over lowering the LGR age limit; an opinion piece by a former equality minister presenting trans people as a threat to gender equality) but has not produced rollback legislation.

sources.claim: Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Sept 2024): Denmark marks 10 years as the first European country with legal self-ID (2014); the debate has stayed cool - no criminal incidents recorded since the law passed, and even a contested prison-placement ruling failed to ignite a political storm. Denmark was also first to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989).

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): robust protections - marriage and adoption, SOGISC discrimination prohibited, self-determined legal gender markers, nonbinary 'X' passports, blood-donation rules based on practices not identity (July 2024), comprehensive LGBTIQ-inclusive sex education; 93% public support for same-sex relationships (Eurobarometer 2023).

TV 2 (Sept 2024, in Danish): Denmark's Supreme Court ruled that a trans prisoner (legally changed gender in 2015, no surgery) must serve her sentence in a men's unit - the case passed without major political controversy.
Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT barometer page on discrimination and hatred - monitoring of discrimination and hate incidents against LGBT people in Denmark.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Denmark: anti-trans and anti-gender discourse intensified during the parliamentary debate on lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition (Christian sites accused trans groups of taking children 'hostage'); the UN Committee Against Torture flagged nonconsensual intersex surgeries; trans people and migrants reported being denied access to spaces and services.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Denmark: former equality minister Marie Bjerre published an opinion piece presenting trans and intersex people as a threat to gender equality (she was reassigned); in July a migrant trans woman was murdered in a Copenhagen hotel room; CAT concerns over intersex surgeries persist.

WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel safety page for Copenhagen (2026): safety confidence scores (LGBTQ+ 91, Trans 89 - 'Safe'); legal status summary (partnerships 1989, marriage 2012, self-declaration since 2014, conversion-therapy ban 2023); describes Copenhagen as compact, walkable and exceptionally safe.
F&M Global Barometers country profile for Denmark: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including the Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

HuffPost (Feb 2013): Fernanda Milan, a Guatemalan trans woman, became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark - she feared persecution for her trans activism in Guatemala (police attacks and threats); initially refused by the refugee appeals board, her case was reopened after LGBT Denmark provided documentation.

records.name: Dominican Republic
records.summary:
The Dominican Republic demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, but strikingly, Articles 210/260 still criminalise it for police and armed-forces members — challenged at the Constitutional Court in August 2024, revealing the institutional culture. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering SOGI (Brazil formally recommended one at the 2024 UPR), and documented violence against trans women is high, particularly affecting the most marginalised.

Tourist zones (Punta Cana, Puerto Plata) are heavily insulated resort enclaves with international norms; Santo Domingo has a visible community and annual Pride caravan. Outside those bubbles, machista culture, police harassment of trans women (especially sex workers), and anti-Haitian dynamics that compound for dark-skinned trans people are documented.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Aug 2024): 'Dominican Republic: Court Reviews Laws Against Gay Sex' — constitutional court hearing challenges to penal-code provisions criminalising same-sex conduct.

UN UPR record (46th session, April 2024): Brazil recommended the Dominican Republic criminalise discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and ensure the right of trans and intersex persons to change name and gender in the civil registry - the recommendation was accepted.

TIME/Amnesty International (March 2019): conversation between two trans activists for Transgender Day of Visibility - including Nairovi Castillo from the Dominican Republic sharing her story of trans life and activism there.
Washington Blade (Apr 2017): Dominican government officials speak at an LGBT conference.
Washington Blade (Apr 2016): opinion — attacks on openly gay US ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster are attacks on LGBT Dominicans.
Washington Blade (Apr 2017): the departure of the gay US ambassador from the Dominican Republic leaves an advocacy void.

freshness.fact: The 2024 constitutional review of the sodomy-law remnants is resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations; still no anti-discrimination or marriage recognition.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in the Dominican Republic

records.name: Algeria
records.summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised, but Cairo 52 documents that it is effectively criminalised through Penal Code Articles 333, 338, and 333 bis (indecency provisions), and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these articles. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years under Article 338. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of Algeria: gender transition is not explicitly criminalised but is effectively criminalised under Articles 333, 338 and 333 bis ('indecency'); no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare means doctors could be prosecuted under Articles 274/264; no legal gender recognition - a court denied a plaintiff's gender correction citing Sharia and Algerian societal norms.

UK Home Office Country Bulletin Algeria: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (July 2026): same-sex activity penalised under Article 338 (up to 2 years) and Article 333 'public indecency' (up to 3 years), applying to men and women; LGBT+ people are a particular social group; those fearing the state are unlikely to obtain protection or relocate internally.

Snopes fact check (Aug 2024): confirms the claim that Algeria prohibits gender transitions and trans identity - homosexuality is criminalised and gender-affirming medical/surgical care is not available; published during the Imane Khelif Olympic controversy.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Algeria: official assessment including the SOGI section - Article 338 criminalises same-sex activity (up to 2 years), Article 333 'public indecency' (up to 3 years); documents arrests and prosecutions of LGBT people.
ILGA 'State-Sponsored Homophobia' world survey (May 2008): global survey of laws criminalising same-sex activity, with Algeria's entry (Articles 333 and 338 of the penal code).
Human Rights Watch (Oct 2020): 'Algeria: Mass Convictions for Homosexuality' — 44 men convicted in a mass case in Constantine, with reports of abusive investigation.

BBC (June 2019): 'The Arab world in seven charts' - Arab Barometer survey of 25,000+ people: acceptance of homosexuality is low or extremely low across the region (Lebanon 6%); rising irreligiosity among youth; Algeria was the exception on women's leadership acceptance - regional social-attitudes context.

records.name: Ecuador
records.summary:
Ecuador demands real caution from trans visitors — a country whose legal framework is now among Latin America's strongest while its streets are among the region's most dangerous. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016; the 2024 Organic Law reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the ID card directly through the Civil Registry (one time, no surgery); and in 2024-25 Constitutional Court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the Assembly for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: Runa Sipiy documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023, with inadequate state response, and the “internal armed conflict” against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024 — two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks. Quito and Guayaquil carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in South America right now.

sources.claim: Primicias (June 2024, in Spanish): President Noboa issued the regulation implementing reforms to the Identity Management and Civil Data Law, allowing people to rectify the sex field or replace it with gender on national ID cards (cédula) via the Civil Registry.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Los Angeles Blade piece (Jan 2024) reports violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians increasing amid the internal armed conflict.
AP (Apr 2026): 'A transgender teen's case in Ecuador opens path for others seeking legal recognition' — Constitutional Court rulings let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex marriage legal since 2019 (adoption still barred by constitutional ban); legal gender recognition since 2016 but not available under 18; conversion practices partially prohibited, with torture-based conversion explicitly criminalised; constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation but gender identity/expression/sex characteristics not explicit; police and prosecutors often fail to investigate hate crimes.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador: documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption - baseline context.

Georgetown Political Database of the Americas: English text of Ecuador's 2008 Constitution - Article 11(2) prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the constitutional framework underpinning LGBT rights in Ecuador.

PinkNews (May 2018): Ecuador's Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register a 7-year-old girl with both mothers' surnames - a historic recognition of LGBT families; context: decriminalisation 1997, civil unions 2015, and a 2016 law allowing people to choose their preferred gender on ID cards; adoption and surrogacy gaps remain.

records.name: Egypt
records.summary:
Egypt is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by Egyptian authorities ("Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here," Cairo 52, 12 incidents 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws (six months + fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (BBC Grindr entrapment) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The Ministry of Interior is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 Universal Periodic Review. The authorities' approach is described as "not only to criminalize LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life."

Egypt has no death penalty for same-sex (unlike Uganda/Nigeria's death penalties), no documented trans-specific tourist killing, and the statutory penalty is six months + fine (not 14 years or life) — but the systematic police entrapment, foreigner-targeting, coerced anal exams, and healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 report 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (Nov 2023) on Egypt's treatment of queer foreigners: analysis of immigration law and 12 incidents (2018-2022). The Ministry of Interior has broad powers to deport or deny entry to anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', interpreted to allow denial of entry and deportation of people perceived as queer; transgender and gender-nonconforming people are most vulnerable to being denied entry.

Cairo 52 (Jan 2024): Egypt's Economic Courts (Alexandria) ruled in multiple cases that Article 25 of the Cybercrime Law explicitly criminalises homosexuality (minimum six months' imprisonment plus fines) - a shift from de facto to explicit criminalisation, interpreted alongside 'debauchery' charges under the 1961 Anti-Sex Work Law.

Cairo 52 (Dec 2024): the Interior Ministry issued a directive to civil registries closing the loophole that had allowed some trans people legal gender recognition via Civil Status Law record-correction committees - intensifying difficulties for trans people who already face a prohibition on gender-affirming healthcare and active criminalisation.

BBC investigation (Jan 2023): how Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps - undercover officers pose online, initiate text conversations, and in some cases allegedly fabricate evidence; the 'debauchery' law (sex-work law) is used to criminalise LGBT people; around half a million British tourists visit Egypt annually and the UK trains Egyptian police via the UN.

Bedayaa Organisation FAQ on the LGBTIQ situation in Egypt: increasing arrests of gay and trans people, coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye to violations, no anti-discrimination law; covers arrests, detention conditions, and the situation of trans persons.

Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, 'The Trap: Punishing Sexual Difference in Egypt' (2017): documents the police's public-morality units tracking LGBTQ people - three patterns: entrapment (especially of trans women) via fake dating-app accounts; deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without upheld charges; and manufactured media 'scandals' (2014 bathhouse raid, 'gay wedding' case).

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): no explicit criminalisation but vague public-morality and 'debauchery' laws used for arrests and prison sentences; dating apps (e.g. Grindr) used for entrapment, with condoms or cash used as evidence of 'habitual debauchery'; the 2018 cybercrime law penalises online content 'threatening family values'; no SOGISC discrimination protection; no legal gender recognition and no functioning pathway to gender-affirming healthcare.
TIMEP/Cairo 52 alternate UPR report (Jan 2025) on Egypt's 4th cycle: discriminatory laws, policies and practices prevent transgender and intersex individuals from enjoying the right to health.

HRW report 'In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct' (Feb 2004): landmark report documenting the Egyptian crackdown - the Queen Boat trial, torture of defendants ('Every place we were held, somebody beat us'), the use of 'debauchery' charges, and the assault on justice through the criminal system.

records.name: Eritrea
records.summary: Eritrea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code criminalises “homosexual conduct” (up to 7 years), there are no anti-discrimination protections of any kind, and Eritrea is among the world's most closed states — indefinite national service, mass arbitrary detention, no independent media, no civil society, and no way to document conditions. Eritrea has rejected every SOGI recommendation at every UPR cycle. Nothing is known about trans people in Eritrea because nothing can be known — the absence of data reflects total informational control.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 310(1) of the 2015 penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' with up to 7 years' imprisonment (inherited from the 1957 Ethiopian code, sentence enhanced at independence). No SOGISC protections; the 2023 US State Department report noted coerced conversion practices to avoid imprisonment and grossly restricted freedoms; no LGBTIQ organisations; queer people remain closeted for fear of imprisonment and violence.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Eritrea: official assessment including the SOGI section - Article 310 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 7 years), coerced conversion practices reported, grossly restricted freedoms.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Eritrea (archived): documents the authoritarian regime's abuses - torture, arbitrary detention, indefinite national service - with the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal stigma.

Asmarino Independent Media (June 2012): reproduction of the US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Eritrea - authoritarian rule under President Afwerki, consistent serious human-rights violations, security forces acting with impunity; includes the LGBT section.

UK FCO 'Eritrea - Country of Concern' report (updated Jan 2015): covers elections, freedom of expression, human-rights defenders, access to justice, death penalty, torture, and freedom of religion - official UK assessment of the human-rights environment.

records.name: Western Sahara
records.summary:
A disputed North African territory under military administration by a neighbouring state, whose penal code governs any visitor: same-sex intimacy is criminalised (six months to three years) with wide police discretion, and morality articles are the tool turned on visibly trans people — rights reviews document involuntary outing, expression discrepancies at checkpoints and registries, no gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition (a 2021 path covers intersex people only); the administering state's religious establishment has condemned transition.

Occupation stacks the risk: 170 charged in the administering state in one year, a 2020 organised outing campaign, rights defenders tried at the territory's own court (a 2005 case of eight Sahrawis remains a landmark), and a 2018 legal study recording LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike. For an outed visitor: criminalisation, morality enforcement and occupation policing, with no civil space and negligible accountability.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of Morocco (applicable to Western Sahara, a disputed territory administered by Morocco): no specific provisions on transition, but trans people face de facto criminalisation under Article 498 (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 legal-recognition process exists for intersex people only; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.

Outright International country overview for Morocco (updated March 2026, applicable to Western Sahara): Article 489 criminalises 'indecent acts' between persons of the same sex (6 months to 3 years), with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; 170 people charged with same-sex relations in 2018; HRW documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; no legal gender recognition; public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment.

Human Rights Watch (Dec 2005): 'Morocco/Western Sahara: Activists Need Fair Trial' — urges fair trial for eight jailed Western Saharan human-rights defenders whose case resumed in Laayoune; general rights context under the administering power.

PinkNews (July 2017): global roundup of countries where homosexuality is illegal - includes Morocco (which administers Western Sahara) with Articles 489/498, fines and up to 3 years' imprisonment; notes vaguely-worded 'morality' laws and unenforced statutes.

CEAR (Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid) report (Oct 2018, in Spanish): 'Situación del colectivo LGTBI en el Sáhara Occidental' - the legal and social status of LGBTI people in Western Sahara, human-rights violations by state and non-state actors, economic/social/cultural rights, and societal attitudes.

records.name: Spain
records.summary:
Spain is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. The 2023 "Trans Law" established legal gender recognition by self-identification and broad anti-discrimination protections, and a parallel penal-code reform made gender identity an explicit hate-crime ground — with real enforcement, including convictions carrying transphobia aggravation. There is no legal restriction on trans people using bathrooms or facilities matching their presentation, and the national tourism industry actively promotes Spain as an LGBTQ destination.

Acceptance is high in cities and tourist regions, though attitudes can be more conservative in some rural areas. Political debate around trans rights is heated, and some regional governments (Madrid, 2023) have rolled back regional protections — signals of a polarised climate rather than changes to a visitor's everyday legal position.

Documented incidents exist: harassment and verbal-abuse prosecutions, a high-profile local-police transphobia case in Benidorm, and gangs targeting queer tourists through dating apps (mainly gay men) in tourist zones — the latter being a general safety caution for app-based meetups anywhere.

sources.claim: Official text (BOE) of Ley 4/2023 (28 February 2023), 'for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGTBI people': establishes self-ID legal gender recognition (16+, no diagnosis), broad anti-discrimination guarantees, employment and health measures, and an LGTBI equality strategy.
Human Rights Watch (Feb 2023): 'Victory in Fight for Gender Recognition in Spain' — hails Spain's self-ID gender-recognition law as a hard-won victory after years of activism.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (June 2026): disentangles three statutes - what Law 4/2023 does and does not do; the discrimination aggravating factor of Article 22.4 of the Penal Code (gender identity/expression motives); and the hate offences of Article 510 CP extended to trans/LGBTI people.

Euro Weekly News (July 2026): contrast piece for expats/travellers - unlike the UK after its Supreme Court ruling, Spain has no legal restriction on trans people using facilities matching their gender; using gendered facilities matching presentation is legal.

Intrepid Travel country guide ('Is Spain safe for LGBTQIA+ travellers?'): Spain is a safe, welcoming destination with marriage equality and protective laws; conservative views persist in rural areas; trans people widely accepted though gender-identity discrimination still occurs.

Turespaña (national tourism institute) B2B page: Spain as a reference destination for LGBTQ+ tourism - inclusive policies, specialised accommodation and events; cites the Homophobic Climate Index and Travel Safety Index ranking Spain among the safest and most welcoming destinations.
La Razón (July 2026, in Spanish): pioneering conviction in Vigo applying the transphobia aggravating factor - WhatsApp threats; €300 fine. Shows the new hate-crime framework is being enforced.

Observatorio de delitos de odio (Jan 2026, in Spanish): six-month prison sentence for a youth gang that pursued, insulted and filmed a trans person in Valencia (including minors among the perpetrators).
UK Foreign travel advice for Spain: safety and security (terrorism threat, crime). General travel advice, not trans-specific.

Wikipedia overview: comprehensive LGBT rights in Spain - same-sex marriage since 2005, adoption, strong discrimination protections, bias-motivated speech/violence provisions, transgender and intersex rights sections, conversion-therapy restrictions, and very positive public opinion.

BuzzFeed News/Ipsos/Williams Institute global survey (Dec 2016) on transgender rights across 23 countries: Spain and Sweden rank at the top for support for trans rights (bathroom access, surgery, marriage, parenting, discrimination protection); one-quarter of Americans say people should never be allowed to change legal gender - comparative public-attitudes data.
